Cancer Survival Mechanisms

Vinata B. Lokeshwar, Ph.D. • Tuesday Lecture 4 • Week 5: Foundations of Cancer Biology

🔥 Professor-emphasis map

The title slide explicitly says red words = high yield and uses a rose icon to mark additional high-yield material. I treated those cues as the professor’s priority system.

  • p53 is a master regulator of cell cycle and survival. The lecture links p53/RB disruption to worse outcomes.
  • Most chemotherapy and radiation affect actively cycling cells, explaining both antitumor effects and injury to rapidly dividing normal tissues.
  • Cancer resists apoptosis by increasing anti-apoptotic proteins and/or reducing pro-apoptotic proteins.
  • Tumor lysis syndrome is a high-yield complication of rapid cancer-cell death: ↑ uric acid, ↑ K+, ↑ phosphate, ↓ Ca2+.
  • Telomerase overexpression enables replicative immortality.
  • Warburg effect: cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis and increase glucose uptake even in the presence of oxygen.
  • Mutant IDH produces 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), an oncometabolite. The lecture marks IDH-targeted AML therapy as high yield.
  • Angiogenesis: tumors require new vasculature once they exceed a very small size; VEGF is a major angiogenic signal.
  • Metastasis is a multistep, inefficient process involving invasion, intravasation, survival, extravasation, and colonization.
  • Treatment resistance reflects cancer stem cells and tumor heterogeneity.
  • Immunotherapy is explicitly labeled “information only” in the learning objectives, so it is summarized but kept lower priority.

Learning Objectives

  1. Understand cancer survival mechanisms (hallmarks of cancer), emphasizing uncontrollable growth, resistance to cell death, and altered metabolism.
  2. Understand why cancer cells achieve immortality and the role of telomerase.
  3. Understand principles of angiogenesis and metastasis.
  4. Understand how the cancer hallmarks form the molecular basis for treatment.
  5. Know the basic concept of immunotherapy as information-only material.

Cancer Hallmarks / Survival Mechanisms

Core idea: cancer cells survive because they acquire multiple coordinated capabilities rather than a single abnormality.
Lecture p. 3 - the lecture centers on sustained growth signaling, evasion of growth suppression, resistance to cell death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion/metastasis, and immune evasion.
Hallmark emphasized in lectureWhat it accomplishes
Sustained growth signalingKeeps proliferative pathways active.
Evade growth suppressionDisables checkpoints and tumor-suppressor pathways.
Resist cell deathAllows damaged cells to survive apoptosis-inducing stress.
Replicative immortalityAvoids telomere-driven senescence.
Altered metabolismProvides rapid energy and biosynthetic intermediates.
AngiogenesisSupplies oxygen/nutrients and removes waste.
Invasion / metastasisAllows local tissue invasion and colonization of distant sites.
Immune evasionPrevents effective antitumor immune destruction.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD

The hallmarks are interconnected. For example, p53 loss can simultaneously promote cell-cycle progression, reduced apoptosis, genomic instability, and treatment resistance. A single driver pathway can therefore affect several “hallmarks” at once.

Uncontrolled Growth and Evasion of Growth Suppression

Normal cell-cycle checkpoints

  • p53 responds to DNA damage and can induce G1 arrest, primarily through p21.
  • p53 can also activate apoptosis when damage is severe.
  • RB restrains G1→S progression by binding E2F.
  • Cyclin D/CDK4/6 phosphorylation of RB releases E2F and allows S-phase gene transcription.
Lecture p. 7 - the rose marker identifies the professor’s high-yield point: p53 is a master regulator of cell cycle and survival.
🔥 PROFESSOR HIGH YIELD

The lecture emphasizes that p53 mutations are common across cancers and associate with metastasis/poor survival; combined p53 and RB disruption is presented as an especially poor-outcome pattern.

⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - p53 / RB logic

p53 → p21 → CDK inhibition → RB stays hypophosphorylated → E2F remains restrained → G1 arrest. Loss of p53 or RB removes a major G1/S checkpoint.

Cell Cycle as a Basis for Cancer Therapy

The lecture emphasizes that most traditional chemotherapy and radiation work because malignant cells are actively proliferating. The tradeoff is injury to normal tissues with rapid turnover.

Common collateral toxicity

  • Bone marrow → myelosuppression, leukopenia/neutropenia, infection, thrombocytopenia, anemia.
  • GI/oral mucosa → nausea, vomiting, mucositis, diarrhea.
  • Hair follicles → alopecia.
Lecture p. 10 - red column headings are explicitly marked high yield. The main study target is the cell-cycle phase, drug, and molecular target.

SMethotrexateDHFR / nucleotide synthesis
SCytarabine, cladribineDNA synthesis
S / G1→SGemcitabineDNA synthesis
S→G2EtoposideTopoisomerase II

⚠️ COMMONLY CONFUSED

Some major agents are cell-cycle nonspecific, including platinum drugs, cyclophosphamide, and anthracyclines in the lecture. They still damage DNA and can ultimately cause cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis.

CDK4/6 inhibitors

The lecture names palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib as therapies that target the Cyclin D-CDK4/6 axis in hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer. Resistance may develop through RB loss or alternative cyclin signaling.

Resistance to Programmed Cell Death

Core idea: cancer survives by shifting the balance away from pro-apoptotic signaling and toward anti-apoptotic signaling.
Lecture p. 12 - cancer resists apoptosis through increased anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL2/BCL-XL/survivin and reduced pro-apoptotic signals such as BAX/PUMA.

Intrinsic vs extrinsic apoptosis

  • Intrinsic: mitochondrial pathway; BCL2-family balance → cytochrome c → caspase-9 → effector caspases.
  • Extrinsic: death-receptor signaling → initiator caspases such as caspase-8 → effector caspases.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - BCL2

BCL2 is anti-apoptotic and prevents mitochondrial cytochrome-c release. Overexpression is classically associated with follicular lymphoma via t(14;18). Venetoclax is a BCL2 inhibitor used in selected hematologic malignancies.

PARP: lecture framing vs board framing

The lecture presents PARP within apoptosis/DNA repair and lists PARP inhibitors as treatment examples in BRCA-mutated gynecologic cancers.

⚠️ BOARD-STYLE REFINEMENT

The most important board concept is that PARP participates in single-strand DNA-break repair. In a BRCA1/2-deficient tumor that cannot effectively repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, PARP inhibition creates synthetic lethality. Do not memorize PARP simply as an “anti-apoptotic protein.”

Lecture p. 13 - this slide is explicitly marked High yield and also repeats the tumor-lysis electrolyte pattern.

Tumor lysis syndrome

Rapid cancer-cell death can release nucleic acids, K+, and phosphate into the circulation.

FindingDirection
Uric acid↑
Potassium↑
Phosphate↑
Calcium↓
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD

TLS can cause acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, seizures, and death. Prevention/treatment centers on hydration and uric-acid control; high-risk or established severe hyperuricemia may require rasburicase.

Replicative Immortality: Telomeres and Telomerase

Normal telomere biology

  • Human telomeres consist of repetitive TTAGGG sequences at chromosome ends.
  • They protect chromosome ends from degradation and end-to-end fusion.
  • Telomeres shorten with repeated cell division.
  • Critically short telomeres trigger chromosome instability and cellular senescence.

How cancer escapes senescence

Cancer cells are constantly dividing, yet many reactivate or overexpress telomerase, which maintains telomeres and permits continued replication.

Lecture p. 16 - telomerase is presented as the answer to tumor-cell immortality.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Telomerase

Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template. It is active in germ cells, stem-cell populations, and many cancers but is low/absent in most mature somatic cells.

Altered Metabolism to Sustain Growth

Warburg effect

Cancer cells show increased glucose uptake and preferential conversion of pyruvate to lactate even when oxygen is available - aerobic glycolysis.

Lecture p. 17 - cancer cells use aerobic glycolysis and show increased glucose and glutamine dependence.

Why aerobic glycolysis can benefit cancer

  • Produces ATP rapidly.
  • Supports survival when oxygen availability fluctuates and tumor cores become hypoxic.
  • Glycolytic intermediates can be diverted into nucleotide, fatty-acid, and methyl-donor biosynthesis.
  • Hypoxia can promote angiogenesis and resistance to chemo/radiation.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - FDG-PET

The Warburg effect explains why many tumors take up large amounts of the glucose analog 18F-FDG. FDG-PET can therefore help detect metabolically active primary and metastatic disease.

Glutamine and a rewired TCA cycle

  • The lecture emphasizes glutamine addiction: glutamine → glutamate → α-ketoglutarate.
  • Cancer cells can use portions of the TCA cycle in nontraditional / “truncated and retrograde” ways to support biosynthesis.

Mutant IDH and 2-hydroxyglutarate

Mutant IDH can convert α-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), an oncometabolite that interferes with α-KG-dependent dioxygenases and alters DNA/histone methylation and differentiation.

Lecture p. 20 - mutant IDH → 2-HG is the central oncometabolite connection.
Lecture p. 21 - the rose icon marks IDH-targeted AML therapy as high yield.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - IDH inhibitors

Ivosidenib targets mutant IDH1; enasidenib targets mutant IDH2. A major toxicity is differentiation syndrome, caused by rapid myeloid maturation and inflammatory cytokine release; glucocorticoids are central to treatment.

Cancer-Associated Cachexia

The lecture defines cachexia as a multifactorial metabolic syndrome with involuntary weight loss, skeletal-muscle wasting (sarcopenia), fatigue, reduced intake, and systemic inflammation.

Lecture p. 23 - tumor- and host-derived inflammatory signals drive anorexia, muscle wasting, and adipose-tissue catabolism.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Cachexia vs starvation

Cachexia is not simply inadequate calorie intake. Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6 increase catabolism and alter metabolism, so nutrition alone may not fully reverse the syndrome.

Angiogenesis

Core idea: diffusion alone cannot support an enlarging tumor, so malignant cells must induce a blood supply.
  • The lecture states tumors cannot grow beyond roughly 2-3 mm without angiogenesis.
  • Angiogenesis = growth of new blood vessels from existing vasculature.
  • An angiogenic switch occurs when proangiogenic factors rise and/or endogenous inhibitors fall.
  • VEGF is a major proangiogenic signal acting on endothelial cells.
Lecture p. 25 - VEGF-driven endothelial signaling and capillary growth are central to the angiogenic switch.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Hypoxia and VEGF

Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1α, which promotes transcription of VEGF and other adaptive genes. Loss of VHL in clear-cell renal cell carcinoma produces inappropriate HIF signaling and strong angiogenic drive.

Antiangiogenic therapy

Lecture p. 26 - examples include anti-VEGF/VEGFR therapies and multitarget kinase inhibitors.
Agent/classLecture targetKey idea
BevacizumabVEGFMonoclonal antibody that neutralizes VEGF signaling.
RamucirumabVEGFR-2Receptor-targeting antibody.
Sunitinib / pazopanibMultikinaseBlock several growth/angiogenic kinase pathways.
Temsirolimus / everolimusmTOR pathwayReduce growth signaling rather than directly neutralizing VEGF.
⚠️ COMMONLY CONFUSED

Not every drug on an “antiangiogenic” regimen directly binds VEGF. Some target VEGFR or upstream/downstream kinase pathways. Know the actual target.

Why antiangiogenic therapy can fail

  • Angiogenesis can resume when treatment stops.
  • Tumors can recruit alternate proangiogenic pathways.
  • Toxicity can limit treatment.
  • Selection pressure promotes resistant subclones.

Metastasis and Treatment Resistance

Metastasis is multistep and inefficient

Lecture p. 28 - primary growth → invasion → intravasation → circulation → extravasation → micrometastasis → colonization.
  1. Primary tumor growth and angiogenic switch.
  2. Loss of contact inhibition / local invasion and basement-membrane breakdown.
  3. Intravasation into blood or lymph.
  4. Survival in circulation; most circulating tumor cells die.
  5. Extravasation at a distant organ.
  6. Micrometastatic survival and colonization to form clinically detectable metastasis.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Invasion machinery

Metastatic cells commonly show loss of E-cadherin-mediated adhesion and increased matrix-degrading enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases, facilitating basement-membrane and extracellular-matrix invasion.

“Seed and soil” concept

The lecture emphasizes that metastasis is organ specific. Successful metastasis requires both a tumor cell capable of dissemination (“seed”) and a distant microenvironment that supports survival (“soil”).

Why metastatic cancer becomes hard to eradicate

Lecture p. 29 - cancer stem cells and tumor heterogeneity are the high-yield explanation for persistent and relapsed disease.
  • Cancer stem cells may divide slowly and survive therapies aimed at highly proliferative cells.
  • Tumor heterogeneity means different subclones have different mutations and drug sensitivities.
  • Treatment kills sensitive cells and selects resistant clones.
  • Resistance can arise by bypass signaling, target modification, loss of tumor suppressors, or new mutations.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Clonal selection

Therapy acts as an evolutionary selection pressure. A previously minor resistant clone can become the dominant population after sensitive clones are eliminated.

Immunotherapy - Information Only

LOW PRIORITY BY LEARNING OBJECTIVE

The lecture explicitly labels immunotherapy as “information only.” Know the concept and major checkpoints, but prioritize the earlier hallmarks for this lecture.

How tumors evade immunity

  • Tumor antigens may be weakly recognized or treated as self.
  • T cells may fail to infiltrate the tumor.
  • Persistent stimulation can cause T-cell exhaustion.
  • PD-L1 on tumor cells can bind PD-1 on T cells and suppress antitumor activity.
  • CTLA-4 is another inhibitory T-cell checkpoint.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Checkpoint inhibitors

Blocking inhibitory checkpoints releases the brakes on T cells. Anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, and anti-CTLA-4 therapies can cause immune-related adverse events resembling autoimmune disease, including dermatitis, colitis, hepatitis, thyroid dysfunction, and other endocrinopathies.

CAR T-cell concept

Patient T cells are genetically modified to express a chimeric antigen receptor that recognizes a tumor-associated surface antigen, expanded, and reinfused to kill antigen-bearing tumor cells.

⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - CAR T toxicities

Important board complications include cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity. Because CAR T therapy targets surface antigens, it is especially established in selected hematologic malignancies.

Rapid Step 1 Review Sheet

p53

Master DNA-damage checkpoint; p21 arrest + apoptosis.

RB

Restrains E2F and G1→S progression.

Chemo toxicity

Hits rapidly dividing marrow, GI mucosa, and hair follicles.

BCL2

Anti-apoptotic; mitochondrial survival signal.

PARP inhibitor

Synthetic lethality in homologous-recombination-deficient tumors.

TLS

↑ uric acid, ↑ K, ↑ phosphate, ↓ calcium.

Telomerase

Reverse transcriptase that maintains telomeres and replicative capacity.

Warburg effect

Aerobic glycolysis with increased glucose uptake and lactate production.

FDG-PET

Exploits high glucose uptake in many tumors.

Mutant IDH

α-KG → 2-HG oncometabolite; blocks normal differentiation/epigenetic regulation.

Ivosidenib

Mutant IDH1 inhibitor.

Enasidenib

Mutant IDH2 inhibitor.

Angiogenesis

VEGF-mediated endothelial growth; HIF-1α rises with hypoxia.

Bevacizumab

Anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody.

Metastasis

Invasion → intravasation → circulation → extravasation → colonization.

Tumor heterogeneity

Distinct subclones enable treatment resistance and relapse.

PD-1/PD-L1

Immune checkpoint suppressing T-cell function.

CAR T

Engineered T cells targeting tumor surface antigens.

Highest-priority “can you explain it out loud?” list

  1. How p53 and RB normally restrain the cell cycle and what cancer gains by losing them.
  2. Why chemotherapy injures both malignant cells and normal rapidly dividing tissues.
  3. How BCL2-family signaling changes the threshold for apoptosis.
  4. The tumor lysis syndrome electrolyte pattern and why it occurs.
  5. Why telomere shortening causes senescence and how telomerase creates replicative immortality.
  6. What the Warburg effect is and why it supports cancer growth and FDG-PET imaging.
  7. How glutamine metabolism and mutant IDH alter cancer-cell metabolism.
  8. Why 2-HG is an oncometabolite and how IDH inhibitors work conceptually.
  9. What cancer cachexia is and why it differs from simple starvation.
  10. Why tumors require angiogenesis and how VEGF/HIF signaling fits.
  11. The steps required for a primary tumor cell to become a clinically established metastasis.
  12. How cancer stem cells and tumor heterogeneity generate treatment resistance.
  13. The basic PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint concepts, recognizing that immunotherapy is lower priority in this lecture.
